items.t: Why do people still get polio in some countries and not in others?
items.x: ( The Conversation ) Why are people still getting polio in some countries and in not others? – Mia, age 9, Centennial, Colorado On a busy street in Karachi, Pakistan, a healthcare worker kneels down so she’s eye to eye with a toddler. She squeezes two drops of liquid onto the child’s tongue. Then she takes out a purple marker and colors the child’s pinkie fingernail so everyone can see that this toddler is now vaccinated against polio. During big vaccination drives, thousands of health workers like her knock on doors across Pakistan. Most kids in the United States will never experience anything like this, because they get the polio vaccine as a shot at the doctor’s office instead of drops in a door-to-door campaign. items.t: NASA telescope is on the verge of plunging back to Earth after failed rescue mission
items.x: CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. (AP) — An aging NASA telescope is barely clinging to space after a failed rescue effort left it tottering lower and lower. The U.S. Space Force predicts the Swift Observatory will come crashing down on or around Friday. Most of the 1 ½-ton telescope is expected to burn up in the atmosphere. But a handful of pieces made of denser-than-lead tungsten and some mirror parts could survive reentry, according to NASA's Brad Cenko, the mission’s chief scientist. Any surviving wreckage will most likely plunge into the ocean. But swaths of Africa, Australia, India, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America are within the reentry zone. The Space Force is tracking the telescope’s dwindling path. items.t: How to tell if a car has a rebuilt title
items.x: ( iSeeCars ) A car’s title is a critical document that not only verifies ownership but also reflects a vehicle’s current status and, potentially, any substantial damage or negative conditions it may have suffered in the past. Two common examples are “rebuilt” and “salvage,” terms indicating that a vehicle was previously declared a total loss or met a state's criteria for salvage status. Let’s take a closer look at what circumstances can lead to a rebuilt title status. What is a rebuilt title? A rebuilt title means the car was previously issued a salvage title, usually after being declared a total loss. It was then repaired and met the state's requirements for a rebuilt title, including any required inspections. items.t: How the law protecting Americans from surprise medical bills is driving up healthcare costs
items.x: ( The Conversation ) Imagine you get hit by a car. An ambulance brings you to the nearest hospital. Your private health insurance covers emergency care, but the hospital isn’t in your plan’s network. Before 2022, if you received emergency care from an out-of-network provider or hospital, you could get hit with an extra, often huge bill on top of what you owe as a copay, coinsurance or deductible. A law called the No Surprises Act , which took effect in 2022, was designed to protect people with private health insurance from just these situations. It limits your costs to what you would have paid if the ambulance had brought you to an in-network hospital or you were treated by an in-network provider instead. items.t: This is the retirement expense you may be underestimating
items.x: People often underestimate some expenses when planning for retirement. In conversations with older adults about their in-retirement finances, they’ve repeatedly mentioned the cost of dental care. The reasons are straightforward: Our teeth get worse as we age, and yet dental care isn’t covered by Medicare (except for emergency dental procedures for people who are hospitalized). There are three main avenues to covering dental costs during retirement: dental insurance, a Medicare Advantage program that covers dental care, and paying out of pocket. Buying stand-alone dental insurance Older adults can purchase stand-alone dental insurance with monthly premiums typically around $25 to $50. Coverage varies widely, however, with plans typically capping the dollar amounts they’ll cover in a year. items.t: How does daylight saving time impact your health?
items.x: ( NewsNation ) – Twice a year, daylight saving time brings a major change to many Americans' schedules, sending clocks back an hour in 48 states. This year, clocks go back an hour on Nov. 1 to standard time. While a 60-minute difference may not seem like much, it has a major impact on many aspects of human life and health. Sleep is impacted, as well as metabolism, mental health and vascular health. Effects can be temporary or long-term. The biannual change has been debated. Dozens of states — and countries — have suggested and pitched legislation for a switch to permanent standard time, which the Society for Research on Biological Rhythms deems "the best option for public health." “The more light exposure you get at the wrong times, the weaker the circadian clock. items.t: Turn this on to stop hackers from stealing your phone number
items.x: ( KTLA ) – Your phone number is more valuable than you might think. It doesn’t just let people call or text you. It can also be the key to getting into your bank accounts, email and other important services. That’s because so many companies still send two-factor authentication codes by text message. If a hacker takes control of your phone number, they could potentially intercept those codes and use them to break into your accounts, KTLA tech reporter Rich DeMuro explains. The attack is called SIM swapping. It happens when someone tricks your wireless carrier into transferring your phone number to a SIM card or eSIM they control. AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon all offer free security features designed to help prevent this. The catch? You typically have to turn them on yourself. Here’s exactly how to do it. The U.S. Space Force predicts the Swift Observatory will come crashing down on or around Friday. Most of the 1 ½-ton telescope is expected to burn up in the atmosphere. But a handful of pieces made of denser-than-lead tungsten and some mirror parts could survive reentry, according to NASA's Brad Cenko, the mission’s chief scientist. items.t: How to tell if a car has a rebuilt title
items.x: ( iSeeCars ) A car’s title is a critical document that not only verifies ownership but also reflects a vehicle’s current status and, potentially, any substantial damage or negative conditions it may have suffered in the past. Two common examples are “rebuilt” and “salvage,” terms indicating that a vehicle was previously declared a total loss or met a state's criteria for salvage status. Let’s take a closer look at what circumstances can lead to a rebuilt title status. What is a rebuilt title? A rebuilt title means the car was previously issued a salvage title, usually after being declared a total loss. It was then repaired and met the state's requirements for a rebuilt title, including any required inspections. items.t: How the law protecting Americans from surprise medical bills is driving up healthcare costs
items.x: ( The Conversation ) Imagine you get hit by a car. An ambulance brings you to the nearest hospital. Your private health insurance covers emergency care, but the hospital isn’t in your plan’s network. Before 2022, if you received emergency care from an out-of-network provider or hospital, you could get hit with an extra, often huge bill on top of what you owe as a copay, coinsurance or deductible. A law called the No Surprises Act , which took effect in 2022, was designed to protect people with private health insurance from just these situations. It limits your costs to what you would have paid if the ambulance had brought you to an in-network hospital or you were treated by an in-network provider instead. items.t: This is the retirement expense you may be underestimating
items.x: People often underestimate some expenses when planning for retirement. In conversations with older adults about their in-retirement finances, they’ve repeatedly mentioned the cost of dental care. The reasons are straightforward: Our teeth get worse as we age, and yet dental care isn’t covered by Medicare (except for emergency dental procedures for people who are hospitalized). There are three main avenues to covering dental costs during retirement: dental insurance, a Medicare Advantage program that covers dental care, and paying out of pocket. Buying stand-alone dental insurance Older adults can purchase stand-alone dental insurance with monthly premiums typically around $25 to $50. items.t: How does daylight saving time impact your health?
items.x: ( NewsNation ) – Twice a year, daylight saving time brings a major change to many Americans' schedules, sending clocks back an hour in 48 states. This year, clocks go back an hour on Nov. 1 to standard time. While a 60-minute difference may not seem like much, it has a major impact on many aspects of human life and health. Sleep is impacted, as well as metabolism, mental health and vascular health. Effects can be temporary or long-term. The biannual change has been debated. Dozens of states — and countries — have suggested and pitched legislation for a switch to permanent standard time, which the Society for Research on Biological Rhythms deems "the best option for public health." “The more light exposure you get at the wrong times, the weaker the circadian clock. Flashing lights, big crowds, and holiday-goers who wear masks and try to spook others can create sensory overload for those kids. You might even see different colored buckets, which signify different disabilities: Teal: Indicates a food allergy. Households can give out no-treat goodies like glow sticks, small toys, and stickers. Blue: Signals a child who is on the autism spectrum. items.t: Turn this on to stop hackers from stealing your phone number
items.x: ( KTLA ) – Your phone number is more valuable than you might think. It doesn’t just let people call or text you. It can also be the key to getting into your bank accounts, email and other important services. That’s because so many companies still send two-factor authentication codes by text message. If a hacker takes control of your phone number, they could potentially intercept those codes and use them to break into your accounts, KTLA tech reporter Rich DeMuro explains. The attack is called SIM swapping. It happens when someone tricks your wireless carrier into transferring your phone number to a SIM card or eSIM they control. AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon all offer free security features designed to help prevent this. The catch? You typically have to turn them on yourself. Here’s exactly how to do it. A judge in Allen Superior Court sentenced 55-year-old Reginald Brooks to 65 years in prison for murder, with 20 more years tacked on for a gun enhancement. items.t: DOJ sentences Wabash man for possessing over 2,000 images of CSAM
items.x: WABASH COUNTY, Ind. (WANE) A man from Wabash, Indiana, has been sentenced to over six years in prison by the Department of Justice for possession of child sex abuse material (CSAM). Friday, the DOJ sentenced 31-year-old Cody Smith to 80 months in prison, or just over six years and six months, followed by another seven years of supervised release. He was also ordered to pay $18,000 in restitution to the victims. Smith was arrested after agents with the Department of Homeland Security executed a search warrant at his home in Wabash. Smith pleaded guilty to his crime.

items.t: Unexplained weight gain and 6 common health problems that can cause it
items.x: Unexplained weight gain, meaning pounds that pile on without any change in diet or activity, often comes from a handful of common health problems. These include an underactive thyroid, polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, heart failure, kidney disease, depression and Cushing’s syndrome. Some of them add fat by changing hormones and metabolism. Others add weight through fluid the body cannot clear. The American Heart Association says people with heart failure should call a doctor if they gain more than 2 to 3 pounds in a day or 5 pounds in a week. Normal daily swings of a few pounds usually come from water and food. The weight worth questioning is the kind that keeps climbing for weeks with no clear reason. googletag.cmd.push(function() { var mapping_lb_1 = googletag.sizeMapping() .addSize([1084, 0], [[300, 250]]) .addSize([0, 0], [[300, 250]]) .build(); googletag.defineSlot('2208318

items.t: Justice Department turns up heat on LA election staff
items.x: The Justice Department has issued federal grand jury subpoenas to election workers in Los Angeles County, ordering at least two employees of the county registrar’s office to appear Nov. 4, the morning after the midterm elections. The registrar’s office confirmed Thursday that the subpoenas were served last week as part of a widening criminal investigation into the Trump administration’s claim that thousands of noncitizens are registered to vote in California. The timing is the story. Federal prosecutors want internal records on how the county screens for noncitizen voters and how it handled federal demands to set aside ballots, and they want them while the same workers are processing mail ballots ahead of Tuesday’s election. The subpoenas surfaced one day after a federal judge refused to let the Justice Department freeze roughly 20,000 California ballots. googletag.cmd.push(function() {

items.t: Will Thanksgiving see snow? Forecasts lean against it
items.x: A strong El Niño is taking shape in the Pacific, and forecasters say it could shape the weather across North America through November and into winter. FOX Weather reports that El Niño is generally not conducive to a widespread white Thanksgiving across the Lower 48. The main question for holiday travelers is whether a possible early breakdown of the polar vortex can override that pattern. Both outlooks rely on models, so the forecast is not settled. What El Niño is doing El Niño describes warmer-than-average water across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. Forecasters say the current event is strengthening quickly, and NOAA expects Super El Niño conditions to develop later this year. Super El Niño status requires water temperatures to stay at least 2 degrees Celsius above normal for three months. items.t: Jumanji crashes into the real world for one last Christmas ride
items.x: For three decades, Jumanji has lived by one unbreakable promise: whatever happens inside the game stays inside the game. This Christmas, that promise shatters. Jumanji: Open World, the closing chapter of Sony's record-setting revival, turns the jungle loose on everyday life, where stampeding rhinos don't come with extra lives, and there's no reset button waiting at the end of a bad level. It is a fitting way to bring the curtain down on a franchise that has quietly become one of Hollywood's most reliable holiday rituals. When Jumanji: Welcome to the Jungle arrived in December 2017, plenty of skeptics wrote it off as a nostalgia play. Audiences answered loudly, pushing the film past $962 million worldwide. Two years later, Jumanji: The Next Level crossed the $800 million mark, cementing the series as a genuine global phenomenon and proving the chemistry between its four leads was no fluke

items.t: Ambulance driver accused of abandoning patient, said he was ‘done driving for the day’ and called an Uber home
items.x: CLEVELAND, Ohio ( WOIO /Gray News) — An ambulance driver is accused of abandoning a patient he was transporting to the hospital earlier this week in Ohio. The incident happened Wednesday evening in Cleveland. The patient was being transported to the Cleveland Clinic with chest pain when the ambulance driver got lost, told her he was done driving for the day, and called an Uber to take him home. The driver worked for a private ambulance company, not for Cleveland EMS. According to Cleveland Association of Rescue Employees (CARE) Local 1975, once the driver left the patient, a Cleveland EMS unit responded to the scene. The paramedics then administered medical care and brought the woman to the hospital, a CARE spokesperson said in a statement . “We stand by our EMTs, paramedics and dispatchers who strive to provide the best care to anyone who is in need of it,” the CARE spokesperson added.

items.t: Bench dedication held for farmer found dead in southeast Mo. in 2025
items.x: SIKESTON, Mo. (Heartland News) - Folks gathered at Veterans Park in Sikeston, Missouri on Saturday morning to remember a local farmer who was found dead in Mississippi County last year . A bench dedication ceremony was held in honor of Gerard Essner on October 31 at 10 a.m. Essner was found dead in October 2025 following a missing person report and homicide investigation. This led to a standoff between a barricaded suspect and several law enforcement agencies. According to Essner’s obituary , he was a retired U.S. Army Veteran and served in the Missouri Army National Guard for 27 years. He created a farming operation alongside his father, Paul, and son, Zachary, named Gerard and Zach Essner Farms. Officer Henry Franklin was killed in the line of duty during this incident . He was also honored with a bench at Veterans Park in Sikeston earlier this year .

TBI said the public’s help remains critical. They reiterated that Jacob Morley is considered dangerous and could be anywhere. Investigators asked the public to remain vigilant, check on family members and neighbors and be alert for any suspicious activity. Jacob Morley is described as between 5-feet, 7-inches and 6-feet tall and weighing between 240 pounds and 270 pounds, with green eyes and brown hair. Boudreau said she has long supported voting, which she described as the right and duty of American citizens to share their voice. “This is the one day that we have to amplify what we want our world to look like, and it just irritated me and my folks, too, when people would say, oh I forgot the election,” Boudreau said. In 1987, Boudreau owned an election supply and voting equipment company. She noticed a county in Washington state had started handing out stickers on Election Day. “It was black and white and had an X in a square. And that’s it. items.t: Police corporal killed in ‘freak’ motorcycle crash remembered by wife, father
items.x: AUTAUGA COUNTY, Ala. ( WSFA /Gray News) - An Alabama woman says she just had two and a half weeks with her husband before he was taken away from her in a motorcycle crash. “I’m waiting for him to walk through the doors,” newlywed bride Chloe Greiner-Davis said. Greiner-Davis’s husband, Dakota Davis, was a corporal with the Prattville Police Department. items.t: Snake Road migration closure extended into November
items.x: UNION COUNTY, Ill. (Heartland News) - The U.S. Forest Service announced that the Snake Road will remain closed until the first week of November. The U.S. Forest Service announced that the Snake Road will now close on November 5. According to Shawnee National Forest authorities, the unseasonably warm weather is causing the snake migration season to lengthen. Each fall, the snakes migrate from their summer habitat in LaRue Swamp to their winter habitat in the limestone bluffs. While the closure means motor vehicles cannot use the road, nature lovers can still walk the snake road to witness the migration first-hand. For more information about the Snake Road hike, visit the U.S. Department of Agriculture website .

items.t: Man posing as Amazon delivery driver accused of stealing multiple packages from neighborhood
items.x: LAKE OSWEGO, Ore. ( KPTV /Gray News) - A Portland man has been arrested after police say he stole packages while posing as an Amazon delivery driver. According to the Lake Oswego Police Department, 51-year-old Ramiro Despaigne Rodriguez was arrested on Oct. 21 after packages were reported stolen from at least eight homes in the Lake Oswego area. Police said the suspect was caught on surveillance video driving a car marked with a “delivery driver” sticker and wearing an Amazon vest. Rodriguez was arrested and booked into the Clackamas County Jail, where he faces first-degree theft charges. Investigators believe there may be more victims connected to this case.

According to the Polk County Sheriff’s Office, deputies served 49-year-old Lakesha Womack with a felony warrant on Oct. 11. Authorities said the warrant was from 2020, charging her with failure to return a hired motor vehicle valued at more than $4,000. items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

Butler authorities say Kayla Dillenburg, 30, strangled a dog she pulled from an Indianapolis shelter, profited from donor pledges meant for its care, and admitted to the killing on a recorded phone call. Dillenburg, who operated Welcome Home Canine Rescue out of her residence, has been charged with torture or mutilation of a vertebrate animal, a felony, and fraud. Court documents stated Dillenburg pulled 21 dogs from Indianapolis Animal Care Services over a 10-day period in late April. Investigators allege she targeted animals carrying high financial pledges raised by social media donors trying to save shelter pets from euthanasia. The woman who died was identified by police as Constance Hages, 31, and family members told authorities she was pregnant. Satellite beacon sent after loss of crampons Forest rangers said the man sent a satellite beacon around 6:30 p.m. after he lost his crampons on an icy ledge. The loss left him stranded. items.t: Jonesboro man accused of stealing from boy scout
items.x: JONESBORO, Ark. (KAIT) - A Jonesboro man was arrested after police said he stole money from a Boy Scout in front of Kroger. Craighead County District Court Judge Tommy Fowler found probable cause Friday to charge Darrick Harris, 19, with aggravated robbery, a Class Y felony, and theft of $1,000 or less, a misdemeanor. What happened at Kroger Officers and a witness recently identified Harris as one of three individuals in video captured at Kroger on Sept. 12. A witness and a juvenile victim said the three individuals worked together to commit the robbery by first approaching the victim’s Boy Scout table and looking it over. The three then entered the store and exited a short time later after they did not purchase any items. Harris and another accomplice went to their nearby bikes and waited as a third approached the victim’s table and threatened him with something he said was in his bag.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access. items.t: When ‘I’ll never put you in a home’ meets real-life caregiving
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Caregiving promises are sometimes made during emotional moments. When a loved one says, “I’ll never put you in a home,” or “You can always live with me,” the words may come from love, but health, safety, money and caregiver capacity can change over time. The Aging Untold experts explain why families may feel guilt or pressure later and what to say instead. Why promises can create pressure Families often make promises before they have talked through what caregiving could involve, Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said. “They haven’t looked at the reality and talked about the reality at first,” O’Rourke said. “You know, ‘I’ll take care of you.’ But if these certain things happen, we’re going to have to have another conversation.” She said the questions can be practical: Can we afford the care? Her pain was on her back and flank. “Not something I could see, not something I could reach, but just an intense amount of burning. And then it came around,” she said. items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Stress can turn into sharp words when you are a caregiver for someone you love. The Aging Untold experts are sharing advice on how to communicate in a way that keeps dignity intact, builds cooperation and helps caregivers reset when a conversation escalates. items.t: Ambulance driver accused of abandoning patient, said he was ‘done driving for the day’ and called an Uber home
items.x: CLEVELAND, Ohio ( WOIO /Gray News) — An ambulance driver is accused of abandoning a patient he was transporting to the hospital earlier this week in Ohio. The incident happened Wednesday evening in Cleveland. The patient was being transported to the Cleveland Clinic with chest pain when the ambulance driver got lost, told her he was done driving for the day, and called an Uber to take him home. The driver worked for a private ambulance company, not for Cleveland EMS. According to Cleveland Association of Rescue Employees (CARE) Local 1975, once the driver left the patient, a Cleveland EMS unit responded to the scene. The paramedics then administered medical care and brought the woman to the hospital, a CARE spokesperson said in a statement . “We stand by our EMTs, paramedics and dispatchers who strive to provide the best care to anyone who is in need of it,” the CARE spokesperson added.

items.t: More than a game: The WWII bond that forever linked Notre Dame and Navy

Since 2011, the teams have played for the Rip Miller Trophy, named after Edgar “Rip” Miller, a former Irish player under the legendary Knute Rockne and a former Navy head coach. The unique prize has two symmetric halves. Each team holds its side, which is inscribed with the team’s captains for that year. The two pieces reunite annually for the rivalry matchup. items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

items.t: ‘I choked that dog out’: Rescue operator charged with felony animal torture
items.x: BUTLER, Ind. ( WPTA /Gray News) - An Indiana woman who operated an animal rescue is facing criminal charges. Butler authorities say Kayla Dillenburg, 30, strangled a dog she pulled from an Indianapolis shelter, profited from donor pledges meant for its care, and admitted to the killing on a recorded phone call. Dillenburg, who operated Welcome Home Canine Rescue out of her residence, has been charged with torture or mutilation of a vertebrate animal, a felony, and fraud. Court documents stated Dillenburg pulled 21 dogs from Indianapolis Animal Care Services over a 10-day period in late April. Investigators allege she targeted animals carrying high financial pledges raised by social media donors trying to save shelter pets from euthanasia. items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

items.t: Detroit organization promotes urban farming amid food insecurity
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Affordability remains the main talking point ahead of the 2026 midterms, and food accessibility is one issue voters may consider when heading to the polls. It’s estimated around 53 million Americans live in what’s called a “food desert,” lower-income areas without easy access to supermarkets or grocery stores. Most of those people live in urban areas, where fast food and convenience shops replace healthy, nutritious foods as the most affordable option. Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access. In Michigan, organizations like the Detroit Black Community Food Sovereignty Network are advocating for urban farming and food sovereignty. items.t: South Bend’s MLK Dream Center unveils new mural
items.x: SOUTH BEND, Ind. (WNDU) - A new mural was unveiled in South Bend’s MLK Dream Center on Friday! The city of South Bend teamed up with the Pokagon Band of Potawatomi Indians and its Four Winds Casinos to unveil the art inside the Dream Center’s gym. The mural displays woodland flowers and the Medicine Wheel, which are native to the Pokagon Band of Potawatomi’s ancestral homelands. The flowers have cultural significance in Potawatomi traditions. They serve as a resource for traditional medicine, markers for planting and harvesting seasons and elements of teaching and ceremonies, according to a news release. The design also weaves in the center’s bright colors and inspirational phrases like “dream it, believe it, achieve it,” underscoring the partnership’s goal of giving people of all ages a place to learn, grow and chase their dreams. Rather than looking solely at party affiliation, political insiders are closely watching three specific demographic groups that could ultimately decide which party controls Congress. Economic headwinds, including agricultural tariffs and the rising cost of everyday essentials like home heating and diesel, are pinching household budgets in rural communities. items.t: How AI is impacting the midterm elections
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - As midterm candidates begin to make their final pitches to voters, experts are speaking out about the impact of artificial intelligence on this election cycle. Chris Borick, a political science professor at Lehigh University, said AI has become a major issue in several races in the last few months. He noted how different the rhetoric surrounding it has been compared to other new technologies. “We like tech traditionally as part of our political economy. That’s really changed in the last year, where you see a much more neutral and sometimes negative political position on AI,” Borick said. items.t: Amish Acres owner arrested in Louisiana on felony warrant
items.x: NAPPANEE, Ind. (WNDU) - The owner of the historic Amish Acres property was arrested Thursday in Louisiana on a felony warrant for issuing worthless checks, according to records. Records show 52-year-old Michael Bradley Loftin, who goes by Brad Juneau, was arrested in Louisiana. A judge ordered him held without bond. The arrest comes more than two months after the state fire marshal shut Amish Acres down over severe fire safety violations . The Indiana Department of Homeland Security released a new report two days later stating that no violations were found at Amish Acres . items.t: More than 42 million Americans have cast early midterm ballots
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - More than 42 million Americans have cast midterm ballots, and interesting demographic data shows who is voting. According to the University of Florida Election Lab , early midterm turnout is similar to the 2018 “blue wave.” The lab said enthusiasm appears to be on the Democrats’ side. Michael McDonald, a University of Florida political scientist, said the U.S. could be headed toward record turnout. “It’s possible that we will beat the 2018 turnout rate. That was the highest turnout rate for midterm elections since 1914. But there are uneven patterns of turnout,” McDonald said. items.t: Man pleads guilty to arson after allegedly trying to set house on fire with mom still inside
items.x: ELKHART COUNTY, Ind. (WNDU) - An Elkhart County man has pleaded guilty to arson after allegedly trying to set his home on fire while his mother was inside . Court records show Christopher Hochstetler entered the plea agreement this week. An attempted murder charge was dismissed as part of the agreement. According to charging documents, Hochstetler told police he really didn’t like his mom when asked why he set the house on fire. Investigators said Hochstetler used a candle lighter and rolled-up toilet paper to start the fire. He placed it next to a wood log in front of his mother’s bedroom, according to the documents. His mother was woken up by a smoke alarm, according to police. Hochstetler is scheduled for sentencing Dec. 3. Stay up to date on local news with WNDU on-air and online. items.x: KOSCIUSKO COUNTY, Ind. (WNDU) - The Indiana Department of Health reported Kosciusko County’s first confirmed measles case this week. Statewide, 97 cases have been reported, including 22 in LaGrange County and three in Elkhart County. Measles is one of the most contagious illnesses. Health officials say people who are not immune have about a 90% chance of becoming infected if they are exposed. “If you didn’t take precautions, you could have a rapid spread,” said Teresa Reed, a communicable disease nurse with the Kosciusko County Health Department. “That’s why there are precautions in place.” State data shows 86.6% of schoolchildren in Kosciusko County have received the measles, mumps and rubella—or MMR—vaccine. items.x: FOXBOROUGH, Mass. (WNDU) - Notre Dame will face Navy at noon tomorrow at Gillette Stadium in the 99th meeting between the Fighting Irish and the Midshipmen dating all the way back to 1927. items.t: Berrien County dentist reaches plea agreement in staff sexual misconduct case
items.x: BERRIEN COUNTY, Mich. (WNDU) - A Berrien County dentist accused of sexually touching his staff has reached a plea agreement. Officials said Charles Howenstine, the former owner of St. Joseph Dentistry, pleaded no contest Thursday, Oct. 29, to one felony count of seduction and two counts of assault and battery. The seduction charge carries up to five years in prison. In Michigan, a no contest plea does not admit guilt. Under state law, it means the defendant is not going to fight the state’s case. According to charging paperwork, the victims, who were dental assistants at St. Joseph Dentistry, gave multiple examples of sexual misconduct, saying Howenstine would regularly touch their buttocks. Another victim reported that Howenstine grazed their thigh while they were treating a patient. Howenstine is scheduled to be sentenced Dec. 7. Then, we discuss clinical trials, why older adults are frequently underrepresented and what questions to ask before participating in a study. Plus, we meet a 91-year-old world record holder in track and field proving that staying active has no age limit. When health changes your sex life, intimacy doesn’t have to disappear Health can affect intimacy as we age and the Aging Untold experts are addressing questions many couples are afraid to ask out loud: When is it safe to resume sex? What if it isn’t? And what should you ask your doctor? Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the first step is figuring out what’s behind the change. items.t: 91-year-old track and field world record holder continues to compete
items.x: SHELBURNE, Vt. ( Aging Untold ) — Flo Meiler began competing in track and field at age 60. She is now 91 and holds two world records, in the pole vault and triple jump. Medals fill Meiler’s home in Shelburne. Most are gold, and a few are silver. How she started Meiler began competing at 60 when her friend Barbara Jordan convinced her to try the long jump at the Vermont Senior Games, and Meiler was hooked. Jordan died a decade ago. “I miss her so much,” Meiler said. Still competing at 91 Meiler continues to compete. “I’m sad that I can’t jump like I used to, but I really enjoy it,” she said. Meiler said it lifts her up when other athletes approach her and tell her she inspires them. “I really feel really warm inside because I’ve had so many athletes come up to me and say, ‘What an inspiration you have been to me,’” she said. “That’s a wonderful feeling.” Inspiring others One of the people

items.t: 103 year-old skydiver
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - A woman in Ohio is proving you can do anything, at any age. At 103-years-old she jumped out of a plane and set the record for the oldest person to ever go skydiving in Ohio.

Four people, all identified as adults, were conscious and taken to a nearby hospital for treatment, according to the El Mirage Police Department. El Mirage Fire Captain Joseph Rivera said one woman was holding an umbrella when lightning struck in the vicinity. The woman reported feeling pain in both of her arms. Capt. Rivera said none of the people were directly struck by the lightning. items.t: Magic water fountain

But what about those kids who bring character, joy, understanding? Our Chad Douglas takes us to a place where teachers use a little whimsy to catapult more students into the spotlight.

One remote control boat, a willing squirrel, and lots of practice launched this amazing act.

items.t: New study reveals 43% drop in childhood peanut allergies over last decade
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Recent research suggests that the long-held medical advice to avoid peanut products for young children may have been exactly the wrong approach. New studies indicate that introducing peanut products to infants between 4 and 6 months old can significantly reduce the risk of developing a peanut allergy. According to a study released in October 2025, peanut allergy rates in children under 3 have dropped by roughly 43% over the last decade. Dr. David Hill, lead author of the study, believes the reversal in guidance is a major factor in this decline. “It’s safe to say in all likelihood, there are tens of thousands of kids today that don’t have food allergy that may have if we hadn’t made these recommendations about early allergen introduction,” Dr. Hill said. items.t: Going trick-or-treating? Here’s some tips for a safe Halloween
items.x: SOUTH BEND, Ind. (WNDU) - Halloween is meant to be fun, but keeping our little ghosts and goblins safe should always come first. Beacon Health System family medicine physicians and pediatricians are encouraging families to make safety a priority. They recommend the following safety tips: Make costumes visible Families should choose light-colored costumes when possible and add reflective tape to costumes, bags and shoes. Children can carry flashlights or glow sticks to help them see and be seen. Costumes should fit properly to help prevent trips and falls. Practice safe trick-or-treating Children should use sidewalks whenever available and cross streets only at intersections and designated crosswalks. items.t: Older adults who stop driving face transportation gaps, experts say
items.x: KANSAS CITY ( InvestigateTV ) — As people age and their health changes, families can face the question of when a loved one should stop driving. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration reports older drivers are more likely than younger drivers to be involved in a car accident. They are “more likely to be seriously hurt,” according to the agency. Most older drivers do not have a plan for when they can no longer drive, which aging experts say is critical. A trip to the doctor without a car Kennie Sandbothe, 77, stopped driving and now relies on a ride program for older adults. Sandbothe was headed to a doctor’s appointment about 25 minutes from their home outside Kansas City. “There’s no buses out here, not in this kind of rural area out here,” Sandbothe said. “It’s so expensive for Uber to take somewhere all the time.” Sandbothe joked that they thought about improvising. “Someti

items.t: Doctor says time outdoors can support physical and mental health
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Spending time in nature can be a healthy reset, according to a doctor who also practices wilderness medicine. Dr. Nathaniel Mann, a Prisma Health emergency doctor, said time spent outdoors is one of the most powerful treatments he has seen, and he supports prescribing it. “Humans, we really didn’t evolve to live in these big structured communities with all the traffic and lights and noise. Our genetic roots are in the outdoors and the surroundings that we see around us right now,” Mann said. Doctor cites human history outdoors Mann spent two years traveling the world, practicing medicine in remote environments. Across his years in medicine, he has found that being outside is one of the most powerful treatments. items.t: Major I-94 project in Berrien County coming to an end, MDOT officials announce
items.x: BERRIEN COUNTY, Mich. (WNDU) - A years-long infrastructure improvement project in Berrien County is nearing an end, Michigan’s Department of Transportation announced. Michigan’s Department of Transportation said the final touches on the nearly 3-year, $204 million project are underway, with all lanes expected to be fully reopened by November 13. The project included rebuilding 8.5 miles of I-94 , including four bridges, between Puetz Road and Britain Avenue. MDOT repaired nine other bridges too. According to MDOT, the project is expected to have directly and indirectly supported 2,911 jobs. Stay up to date on local news with WNDU on-air and online. items.x: FOREST CITY, N.C. ( WHNS /Gray News) – A round of drinks turned into a medical nightmare when three customers ordered margaritas and immediately suffered chemical burns inside and around their mouths. Health officials investigating the incident at a Chili’s Grill & Bar in Forest City, North Carolina, said the drinks were contaminated after a powerful industrial degreaser was mistaken for sugar. The dangerous mix-up began when a restaurant worker obtained granulated degreasing agent from an outside contractor power-washing the building’s exterior, according to the Foothills Health District. The employee poured the chemical into an unlabeled container, brought it inside and left it in the bar area. items.t: Dating again? What older adults should know about sexual health and protection
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Dating, intimacy and connection can be an important part of emotional and physical well-being for older adults. That includes people who are divorced, widowed, remarried or dating again for the first time in decades. The Aging Untold experts are addressing the topics of sexual health, how it has changed over the years and how to stay protected. items.x: (Gray News) - Ground cinnamon is being recalled in 14 states ahead of the holiday season. SLR Food Distribution Inc said it’s voluntarily recalling Wise Wife Brand Ground Cinnamon because it could be contaminated with elevated levels of lead, according to a recall alert. According to the recall notice, lead exposure can impact nearly every bodily system, with effects depending on dosage, duration, and an individual’s age and weight. Low-level, short-term exposure may not produce immediate symptoms, and no illnesses have been reported to date. items.t: Police respond to reported stabbing in South Bend
items.x: SOUTH BEND, Ind. (WNDU) - Police responded to a reported stabbing this morning in the 2300 block of N. Bendix Drive at Beacon Occupational Health, according to St. Joseph County dispatchers. items.t: When ‘I’ll never put you in a home’ meets real-life caregiving
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Caregiving promises are sometimes made during emotional moments. When a loved one says, “I’ll never put you in a home,” or “You can always live with me,” the words may come from love, but health, safety, money and caregiver capacity can change over time. The Aging Untold experts explain why families may feel guilt or pressure later and what to say instead. Why promises can create pressure Families often make promises before they have talked through what caregiving could involve, Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said. “They haven’t looked at the reality and talked about the reality at first,” O’Rourke said. “You know, ‘I’ll take care of you.’ But if these certain things happen, we’re going to have to have another conversation.” She said the questions can be practical: Can we afford the care? items.t: ‘Bad houseguest’ in the attic: What to know about shingles symptoms and treatments
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Many people think the first sign of shingles is a bad rash, but it can start with intense pain in the body. ‘Intense amount of burning’ Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said she had shingles twice and it was tied to an autoimmune condition, and described the pain as burning. “It burned. It’s an infection in the nerve, essentially. It is nerve pain at the highest level,” Cradduck said. She compared it to a toothache. “You know how intense a toothache is. Now think about that in a pathway, in a nerve pathway in your body,” Cradduck said. Her pain was on her back and flank. “Not something I could see, not something I could reach, but just an intense amount of burning. And then it came around,” she said. items.t: Better than blood? Researcher says new discovery could help save lives
items.x: KANSAS CITY, Mo. ( InvestigateTV ) — A doctor and research scientist at the University of Missouri-Kansas City said he has discovered a potential alternative to blood transfusions for people with severe blood loss. He calls the treatment “better than blood.” When someone experiences severe trauma, such as a car crash or gunshot wound, they risk bleeding to death. Blood transfusions are currently the best treatment to try to stop severe blood loss, also known as hemorrhagic shock. How the discovery happened Dr. Cuthbert Simpkins, founder of Vivacelle Bio, said he was running an experiment he thought would fail. “But it didn’t fail.” For years, Simpkins, who is now a surgery professor at the UKMC School of Medicine, had been trying to find an answer for septic shock and focused his research on blood experiments. items.t: How caregivers can keep dignity intact when conversations get tense
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Stress can turn into sharp words when you are a caregiver for someone you love. The Aging Untold experts are sharing advice on how to communicate in a way that keeps dignity intact, builds cooperation and helps caregivers reset when a conversation escalates. Step away before things escalate “Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the first move to make when it feels like a conversation is about to escalate is to leave the room. “You have to step away. You really do,” Cradduck said. “You’ve got to let yourself calm down.” Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said caregivers can take that step by removing themselves or getting help. “If you’re fantasizing about escaping, or noticing the yellow flags like you’re starting to get hot, shaky, your jaw’s tense, that’s a good time to go, ‘OK, my nervous system is at its limit,’” Ambrose said. items.t: What to look for in a clinical trial and why older adults should be included
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Clinical trials can be a proactive way to explore new treatments, but studies show older adults are often left out of them, even though many conditions affect older adults more often. The Aging Untold experts hosts are discussing what to look for when choosing a study and how to decide whether to take part. Start with the question the trial is trying to answer Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the first step is to change the question you ask. “I think the first thing we have to do is not think about, ‘Can this clinical trial help me?’ but ‘What is this clinical trial trying to answer?’” Rogers said. “That’s what most of these trials are about.” A trial is not a last resort Rogers said many people see clinical trials as a last resort. “I think a lot of people think that it’s a last resort option, that you don’t have anything else, when in fact one of th

items.x: WILMINGTON, N.C. ( InvestigateTV ) — Some doctors and caregivers are using art to help people with memory loss stay calm, engaged and connected. Research published by the National Library of Medicine shows drawing and painting can sometimes stimulate memories in people with dementia and other neurological diseases. Mother and daughter paint together June Lederle and her daughter, Cathie Lederle, create artwork at a table in their Wilmington home most days. On the day of the interview, Cathie was painting a bottle purple, the color of Alzheimer’s awareness. Before moving in with her mother, Cathie lived in Richmond, Virginia, and had a career in a technical field. June said the first signs that something was wrong appeared in 2019, starting with forgetfulness and then repeating tasks. Cognitive testing later confirmed their fears. items.t: Ambulance driver accused of abandoning patient, said he was ‘done driving for the day’ and called an Uber home
items.x: CLEVELAND, Ohio ( WOIO /Gray News) — An ambulance driver is accused of abandoning a patient he was transporting to the hospital earlier this week in Ohio. The incident happened Wednesday evening in Cleveland. The patient was being transported to the Cleveland Clinic with chest pain when the ambulance driver got lost, told her he was done driving for the day, and called an Uber to take him home. The driver worked for a private ambulance company, not for Cleveland EMS. According to Cleveland Association of Rescue Employees (CARE) Local 1975, once the driver left the patient, a Cleveland EMS unit responded to the scene. The paramedics then administered medical care and brought the woman to the hospital, a CARE spokesperson said in a statement . “We stand by our EMTs, paramedics and dispatchers who strive to provide the best care to anyone who is in need of it,” the CARE spokesperson added.

items.t: Fatal motorcycle crash closes roadway in Clarksville
items.x: CLARKSVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV) - The Clarksville Police Department said it is investigating a fatal motorcycle crash Saturday afternoon. CPD said the crash happened on Excell Road at Farmers Road around 3:11 p.m. The crash has completely closed Excell Road as police investigate. It is not clear the number of injuries or fatalities at this time, but CPD said injuries were involved. “Motorists are advised to avoid the area and find an alternate route until the roadway is cleared,” CPD said. This is a developing story.

items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

items.t: 91-year-old track and field world record holder continues to compete
items.x: SHELBURNE, Vt. ( Aging Untold ) — Flo Meiler began competing in track and field at age 60. She is now 91 and holds two world records, in the pole vault and triple jump. Medals fill Meiler’s home in Shelburne. Most are gold, and a few are silver. How she started Meiler began competing at 60 when her friend Barbara Jordan convinced her to try the long jump at the Vermont Senior Games, and Meiler was hooked. Jordan died a decade ago. “I miss her so much,” Meiler said. Still competing at 91 Meiler continues to compete. “I’m sad that I can’t jump like I used to, but I really enjoy it,” she said. Meiler said it lifts her up when other athletes approach her and tell her she inspires them. “I really feel really warm inside because I’ve had so many athletes come up to me and say, ‘What an inspiration you have been to me,’” she said. “That’s a wonderful feeling.” Inspiring others One of the people

items.t: New study reveals 43% drop in childhood peanut allergies over last decade
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Recent research suggests that the long-held medical advice to avoid peanut products for young children may have been exactly the wrong approach. New studies indicate that introducing peanut products to infants between 4 and 6 months old can significantly reduce the risk of developing a peanut allergy. According to a study released in October 2025, peanut allergy rates in children under 3 have dropped by roughly 43% over the last decade. Dr. David Hill, lead author of the study, believes the reversal in guidance is a major factor in this decline. “It’s safe to say in all likelihood, there are tens of thousands of kids today that don’t have food allergy that may have if we hadn’t made these recommendations about early allergen introduction,” Dr. Hill said. Dr. Nathaniel Mann, a Prisma Health emergency doctor, said time spent outdoors is one of the most powerful treatments he has seen, and he supports prescribing it. “Humans, we really didn’t evolve to live in these big structured communities with all the traffic and lights and noise. Our genetic roots are in the outdoors and the surroundings that we see around us right now,” Mann said. Doctor cites human history outdoors Mann spent two years traveling the world, practicing medicine in remote environments. Across his years in medicine, he has found that being outside is one of the most powerful treatments. items.t: When ‘I’ll never put you in a home’ meets real-life caregiving
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Caregiving promises are sometimes made during emotional moments. When a loved one says, “I’ll never put you in a home,” or “You can always live with me,” the words may come from love, but health, safety, money and caregiver capacity can change over time. items.t: ‘Bad houseguest’ in the attic: What to know about shingles symptoms and treatments
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Many people think the first sign of shingles is a bad rash, but it can start with intense pain in the body. ‘Intense amount of burning’ Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said she had shingles twice and it was tied to an autoimmune condition, and described the pain as burning. “It burned. It’s an infection in the nerve, essentially. It is nerve pain at the highest level,” Cradduck said. She compared it to a toothache. “You know how intense a toothache is. Now think about that in a pathway, in a nerve pathway in your body,” Cradduck said. Her pain was on her back and flank. “Not something I could see, not something I could reach, but just an intense amount of burning. And then it came around,” she said. items.x: KANSAS CITY, Mo. ( InvestigateTV ) — A doctor and research scientist at the University of Missouri-Kansas City said he has discovered a potential alternative to blood transfusions for people with severe blood loss. He calls the treatment “better than blood.” When someone experiences severe trauma, such as a car crash or gunshot wound, they risk bleeding to death. Blood transfusions are currently the best treatment to try to stop severe blood loss, also known as hemorrhagic shock. items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

The patient was being transported to the Cleveland Clinic with chest pain when the ambulance driver got lost, told her he was done driving for the day, and called an Uber to take him home. items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access. items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

Some believed it was a vampire beast because it crushed its prey’s skulls and drained their blood. “We didn’t have that many residents at that time, maybe 700 or 800 people but the population grew to 1,200 people or more because hunters came to hunt the beast,” Walters said. items.t: 91-year-old track and field world record holder continues to compete

Medals fill Meiler’s home in Shelburne. Most are gold, and a few are silver. How she started Meiler began competing at 60 when her friend Barbara Jordan convinced her to try the long jump at the Vermont Senior Games, and Meiler was hooked. Jordan died a decade ago. “I miss her so much,” Meiler said. Still competing at 91 Meiler continues to compete. “I’m sad that I can’t jump like I used to, but I really enjoy it,” she said. Meiler said it lifts her up when other athletes approach her and tell her she inspires them. “I really feel really warm inside because I’ve had so many athletes come up to me and say, ‘What an inspiration you have been to me,’” she said. “That’s a wonderful feeling.” Inspiring others One of the people

items.t: New study reveals 43% drop in childhood peanut allergies over last decade
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Recent research suggests that the long-held medical advice to avoid peanut products for young children may have been exactly the wrong approach. New studies indicate that introducing peanut products to infants between 4 and 6 months old can significantly reduce the risk of developing a peanut allergy. ( InvestigateTV ) — A doctor and research scientist at the University of Missouri-Kansas City said he has discovered a potential alternative to blood transfusions for people with severe blood loss. He calls the treatment “better than blood.” When someone experiences severe trauma, such as a car crash or gunshot wound, they risk bleeding to death. Blood transfusions are currently the best treatment to try to stop severe blood loss, also known as hemorrhagic shock. How the discovery happened Dr. Cuthbert Simpkins, founder of Vivacelle Bio, said he was running an experiment he thought would fail. “But it didn’t fail.” For years, Simpkins, who is now a surgery professor at the UKMC School of Medicine, had been trying to find an answer for septic shock and focused his research on blood experiments. items.t: How caregivers can keep dignity intact when conversations get tense
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Stress can turn into sharp words when you are a caregiver for someone you love. The Aging Untold experts are sharing advice on how to communicate in a way that keeps dignity intact, builds cooperation and helps caregivers reset when a conversation escalates. Step away before things escalate “Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the first move to make when it feels like a conversation is about to escalate is to leave the room. “You have to step away. You really do,” Cradduck said. “You’ve got to let yourself calm down.” Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said caregivers can take that step by removing themselves or getting help. “If you’re fantasizing about escaping, or noticing the yellow flags like you’re starting to get hot, shaky, your jaw’s tense, that’s a good time to go, ‘OK, my nervous system is at its limit,’” Ambrose said. items.t: What to look for in a clinical trial and why older adults should be included
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Clinical trials can be a proactive way to explore new treatments, but studies show older adults are often left out of them, even though many conditions affect older adults more often. The Aging Untold experts hosts are discussing what to look for when choosing a study and how to decide whether to take part. Start with the question the trial is trying to answer Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the first step is to change the question you ask. “I think the first thing we have to do is not think about, ‘Can this clinical trial help me?’ but ‘What is this clinical trial trying to answer?’” Rogers said. “That’s what most of these trials are about.” A trial is not a last resort Rogers said many people see clinical trials as a last resort. “I think a lot of people think that it’s a last resort option, that you don’t have anything else, when in fact one of th

items.x: WILMINGTON, N.C. ( InvestigateTV ) — Some doctors and caregivers are using art to help people with memory loss stay calm, engaged and connected. Research published by the National Library of Medicine shows drawing and painting can sometimes stimulate memories in people with dementia and other neurological diseases. Mother and daughter paint together June Lederle and her daughter, Cathie Lederle, create artwork at a table in their Wilmington home most days. On the day of the interview, Cathie was painting a bottle purple, the color of Alzheimer’s awareness. Before moving in with her mother, Cathie lived in Richmond, Virginia, and had a career in a technical field. June said the first signs that something was wrong appeared in 2019, starting with forgetfulness and then repeating tasks. Cognitive testing later confirmed their fears. items.t: Ambulance driver accused of abandoning patient, said he was ‘done driving for the day’ and called an Uber home
items.x: CLEVELAND, Ohio ( WOIO /Gray News) — An ambulance driver is accused of abandoning a patient he was transporting to the hospital earlier this week in Ohio. The incident happened Wednesday evening in Cleveland. The patient was being transported to the Cleveland Clinic with chest pain when the ambulance driver got lost, told her he was done driving for the day, and called an Uber to take him home. The driver worked for a private ambulance company, not for Cleveland EMS. According to Cleveland Association of Rescue Employees (CARE) Local 1975, once the driver left the patient, a Cleveland EMS unit responded to the scene. The paramedics then administered medical care and brought the woman to the hospital, a CARE spokesperson said in a statement . “We stand by our EMTs, paramedics and dispatchers who strive to provide the best care to anyone who is in need of it,” the CARE spokesperson added.

items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access. items.x: JACKSON, Miss. (WLBT) — Most of the state, including Hinds County, is under a burn ban, but a string of fires has broken out across the city of Jackson. The Jackson Fire Department said the city has seen an influx of fires in the past few weeks and is asking residents to help prevent them. Some of the fires are being investigated as arson, and officials said others started because of simple carelessness. Officials said that under the current burn ban, even a small spark can lead to a felony charge. Jackson Fire Chief RaSean O. Thomas said people are responsible for the fires they cause. “If you throw a cigarette butt out of the window, and you cause a fire, you can burn someone’s home, you can burn someone’s property,” Thomas said. “… That is part of your responsibility to make sure you dispose of it properly. Medals fill Meiler’s home in Shelburne. Most are gold, and a few are silver. items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

items.x: TALLAHASSEE, Fla. (WCTV) - Thunderstorms can be difficult to predict, and once the sun sets, the degree of difficulty ramps up. A Florida State University assistant professor is attempting to tackle the challenge with a new project. Dr. Hristo Chipilski received a nearly $500,000 grant from the National Science Foundation to blend real-time atmospheric measurements with advanced computer algorithms, aiming to establish a more accurate starting point for numerical forecast models. “During the nighttime, there is no sun. items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Spending time in nature can be a healthy reset, according to a doctor who also practices wilderness medicine. Dr. Nathaniel Mann, a Prisma Health emergency doctor, said time spent outdoors is one of the most powerful treatments he has seen, and he supports prescribing it. “Humans, we really didn’t evolve to live in these big structured communities with all the traffic and lights and noise. items.x: DORCHESTER COUNTY, S.C. (WCSC) — The Dorchester County Water and Sewer Department has lifted a boil water advisory for customers in portions of the Coosaw Creek neighborhood. items.t: Ambulance driver accused of abandoning patient, said he was ‘done driving for the day’ and called an Uber home
items.x: CLEVELAND, Ohio ( WOIO /Gray News) — An ambulance driver is accused of abandoning a patient he was transporting to the hospital earlier this week in Ohio. The incident happened Wednesday evening in Cleveland. The patient was being transported to the Cleveland Clinic with chest pain when the ambulance driver got lost, told her he was done driving for the day, and called an Uber to take him home. The driver worked for a private ambulance company, not for Cleveland EMS. According to Cleveland Association of Rescue Employees (CARE) Local 1975, once the driver left the patient, a Cleveland EMS unit responded to the scene. The paramedics then administered medical care and brought the woman to the hospital, a CARE spokesperson said in a statement . “We stand by our EMTs, paramedics and dispatchers who strive to provide the best care to anyone who is in need of it,” the CARE spokesperson added.
