items.t: When ‘I’ll never put you in a home’ meets real-life caregiving
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Caregiving promises are sometimes made during emotional moments. When a loved one says, “I’ll never put you in a home,” or “You can always live with me,” the words may come from love, but health, safety, money and caregiver capacity can change over time. The Aging Untold experts explain why families may feel guilt or pressure later and what to say instead. Why promises can create pressure Families often make promises before they have talked through what caregiving could involve, Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said. “They haven’t looked at the reality and talked about the reality at first,” O’Rourke said. “You know, ‘I’ll take care of you.’ But if these certain things happen, we’re going to have to have another conversation.” She said the questions can be practical: Can we afford the care? items.t: ‘Bad houseguest’ in the attic: What to know about shingles symptoms and treatments
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Many people think the first sign of shingles is a bad rash, but it can start with intense pain in the body. ‘Intense amount of burning’ Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said she had shingles twice and it was tied to an autoimmune condition, and described the pain as burning. “It burned. It’s an infection in the nerve, essentially. It is nerve pain at the highest level,” Cradduck said. She compared it to a toothache. “You know how intense a toothache is. Now think about that in a pathway, in a nerve pathway in your body,” Cradduck said. Her pain was on her back and flank. “Not something I could see, not something I could reach, but just an intense amount of burning. And then it came around,” she said. ( InvestigateTV ) — A doctor and research scientist at the University of Missouri-Kansas City said he has discovered a potential alternative to blood transfusions for people with severe blood loss. He calls the treatment “better than blood.” When someone experiences severe trauma, such as a car crash or gunshot wound, they risk bleeding to death. items.t: How caregivers can keep dignity intact when conversations get tense
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Stress can turn into sharp words when you are a caregiver for someone you love. The Aging Untold experts are sharing advice on how to communicate in a way that keeps dignity intact, builds cooperation and helps caregivers reset when a conversation escalates. Step away before things escalate “Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the first move to make when it feels like a conversation is about to escalate is to leave the room. “You have to step away. The incident happened Wednesday evening in Cleveland. The patient was being transported to the Cleveland Clinic with chest pain when the ambulance driver got lost, told her he was done driving for the day, and called an Uber to take him home. items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access. items.t: Moment of Science: The science behind your scream
items.x: COLUMBIA, S.C. (WIS) - Fear is instilled in all of us, but it varies from person to person. Like most reactions, fear starts in the brain. Your amygdala, located behind your eyes and between your ears, is an almond-shaped cluster of cells. It’s a primary emotional processor, picking up on other emotions and linking them to different senses, including fear. Historically, humans have needed fear to avoid danger altogether and survive. Some fears and anxieties can be genetic, but the situation controls your emotions. Let’s say you’re on the riverwalk and you encounter a bear. Immediately, your amygdala gets to work, signaling your hypothalamus to produce stress hormones such as adrenaline. Simultaneously, your hippocampus triggers a “fight or flight” response. items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

items.t: Halloween 2026 statistics and forecast
items.x: BISMARCK, N.D. (KFYR) - Halloween weather heavily shapes trick-or-treating plans, costume choices, and more. Here are some very spooky statistics for this weather-dependent holiday. Halloween falls in one of the most volatile months of the year. We’ve had years with cold and snow, but we’ve also had pretty nice Halloweens. In the last five years, we’ve seen it all. Last Halloween was a little chilly, with highs in the 30s and 40s. We had near normal temperatures in 2024 and 2021. The big jumps were back-to-back years of 2023 and 2022; from warm and well above normal temps in 2022 to cold, well below normal temps in 2023. You can see the differences even more per city. Take Bismarck for example: a record high of 7 degrees and a record low of 10 degrees below zero! Last year was pretty close to normal. Or Minot: the record temperatures are not as big of a swing, but more for a record snow.

items.t: Experts eye key voting blocs ahead of Midterms
items.x: NEW YORK CITY (Gray Media) - With millions of ballots already cast ahead of Election Day, conversations surrounding voter turnout are intensifying. Rather than looking solely at party affiliation, political insiders are closely watching three specific demographic groups that could ultimately decide which party controls Congress. items.t: What to look for in a clinical trial and why older adults should be included
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Clinical trials can be a proactive way to explore new treatments, but studies show older adults are often left out of them, even though many conditions affect older adults more often. Before moving in with her mother, Cathie lived in Richmond, Virginia, and had a career in a technical field. items.t: Ambulance driver accused of abandoning patient, said he was ‘done driving for the day’ and called an Uber home
items.x: CLEVELAND, Ohio ( WOIO /Gray News) — An ambulance driver is accused of abandoning a patient he was transporting to the hospital earlier this week in Ohio. The incident happened Wednesday evening in Cleveland. The patient was being transported to the Cleveland Clinic with chest pain when the ambulance driver got lost, told her he was done driving for the day, and called an Uber to take him home. The driver worked for a private ambulance company, not for Cleveland EMS. According to Cleveland Association of Rescue Employees (CARE) Local 1975, once the driver left the patient, a Cleveland EMS unit responded to the scene. The paramedics then administered medical care and brought the woman to the hospital, a CARE spokesperson said in a statement . “We stand by our EMTs, paramedics and dispatchers who strive to provide the best care to anyone who is in need of it,” the CARE spokesperson added.

Data from the South Carolina Election Commission shows that 110,172 votes were cast on Friday, bringing the statewide total to 948,592. The cumulative total is the highest early turnout for a gubernatorial election since the state began offering early voting in 2022. items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

Most of those people live in urban areas, where fast food and convenience shops replace healthy, nutritious foods as the most affordable option. Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access. In Michigan, organizations like the Detroit Black Community Food Sovereignty Network are advocating for urban farming and food sovereignty. items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

items.t: How AI is impacting the midterm elections
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - As midterm candidates begin to make their final pitches to voters, experts are speaking out about the impact of artificial intelligence on this election cycle. Chris Borick, a political science professor at Lehigh University, said AI has become a major issue in several races in the last few months. items.t: More than 42 million Americans have cast early midterm ballots
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - More than 42 million Americans have cast midterm ballots, and interesting demographic data shows who is voting. According to the University of Florida Election Lab , early midterm turnout is similar to the 2018 “blue wave.” The lab said enthusiasm appears to be on the Democrats’ side. Michael McDonald, a University of Florida political scientist, said the U.S. could be headed toward record turnout. “It’s possible that we will beat the 2018 turnout rate. That was the highest turnout rate for midterm elections since 1914. But there are uneven patterns of turnout,” McDonald said. McDonald said the uneven turnout levels come from a partisan divide. “Registered Democrats, unaffiliated, those people who don’t have a party registration, are engaged at the moment. items.t: Georgia state troopers can now take digital driver’s licenses, safety department says
items.x: ATLANTA, Ga. (Atlanta News First) — The public can now present a digital driver’s license or ID to Georgia Department of Safety officers, the agency announced on Friday. During traffic stops, crash investigations or other encounters, all state troopers, Commercial Vehicle Enforcement officers and Capitol police officers will now be able to scan the digital ID. The department says you can tell the officer you’d like to use your digital license and hold your device near the identity reader. Don’t give your device to the officer, officials added. The update follows H.B. 296, a bill signed in 2025 that requires police to be able to verify electronic licenses by July 1, 2027. The department recommends the public still carry their physical ID as well. Click here to learn more about what a Georgia digital driver’s license and ID is and how to get one. items.t: 91-year-old track and field world record holder continues to compete
items.x: SHELBURNE, Vt. ( Aging Untold ) — Flo Meiler began competing in track and field at age 60. She is now 91 and holds two world records, in the pole vault and triple jump. Medals fill Meiler’s home in Shelburne. Most are gold, and a few are silver. How she started Meiler began competing at 60 when her friend Barbara Jordan convinced her to try the long jump at the Vermont Senior Games, and Meiler was hooked. Jordan died a decade ago. “I miss her so much,” Meiler said. Still competing at 91 Meiler continues to compete. “I’m sad that I can’t jump like I used to, but I really enjoy it,” she said. Meiler said it lifts her up when other athletes approach her and tell her she inspires them. “I really feel really warm inside because I’ve had so many athletes come up to me and say, ‘What an inspiration you have been to me,’” she said. “That’s a wonderful feeling.” Inspiring others One of the people

items.t: New study reveals 43% drop in childhood peanut allergies over last decade
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Recent research suggests that the long-held medical advice to avoid peanut products for young children may have been exactly the wrong approach. New studies indicate that introducing peanut products to infants between 4 and 6 months old can significantly reduce the risk of developing a peanut allergy. According to a study released in October 2025, peanut allergy rates in children under 3 have dropped by roughly 43% over the last decade. Dr. David Hill, lead author of the study, believes the reversal in guidance is a major factor in this decline. “It’s safe to say in all likelihood, there are tens of thousands of kids today that don’t have food allergy that may have if we hadn’t made these recommendations about early allergen introduction,” Dr. Hill said. items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before this weekend’s time change.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Affordability remains the main talking point ahead of the 2026 midterms, and food accessibility is one issue voters may consider when heading to the polls. It’s estimated around 53 million Americans live in what’s called a “food desert,” lower-income areas without easy access to supermarkets or grocery stores. Most of those people live in urban areas, where fast food and convenience shops replace healthy, nutritious foods as the most affordable option. Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access. In Michigan, organizations like the Detroit Black Community Food Sovereignty Network are advocating for urban farming and food sovereignty. items.t: Experts eye key voting blocs ahead of Midterms
items.x: NEW YORK CITY (Gray Media) - With millions of ballots already cast ahead of Election Day, conversations surrounding voter turnout are intensifying. Rather than looking solely at party affiliation, political insiders are closely watching three specific demographic groups that could ultimately decide which party controls Congress. Economic headwinds, including agricultural tariffs and the rising cost of everyday essentials like home heating and diesel, are pinching household budgets in rural communities. While Mitchell does not expect these voters to dramatically flip parties, financial strain could depress turnout or weaken enthusiasm for Republicans and President Donald Trump. items.t: Daimler closes truck manufacturing plant in north Portland; Lays off 375 workers
items.x: PORTLAND Ore. (KPTV) - A truck manufacturing plant in northwest Portland closed for good on Friday, laying off almost 400 workers. Daimler Truck North America made the announcement in July, saying 375 positions would be eliminated. In July, the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers union issued a statement in response: “Our employer’s decision to leave the Portland area does not remove the heart and soul that our members have put into their work at Daimler. And the IAM will support and fight for our members regardless of any decision their employer makes.” Officials at Daimler say while their Portland factory is closing, the city will continue to serve as their North American headquarters. Production will be moved to Daimler’s facilities in the Carolinas.

items.t: Oregon Zoo treating Tula-Tu for virus that killed another baby elephant
items.x: PORTLAND Ore. (KPTV) - Veterinary teams at the Oregon Zoo have started intensive treatment for an Asian elephant calf, Tula-Tu, infected with elephant endotheliotropic herpesvirus, or EEHV. Staff noticed changes in the behavior and energy levels of the calf, Tula-Tu, on Oct. 24. Technicians found a low white blood cell count during routine in-house screening, prompting veterinarians to start antiviral medications immediately, the zoo said in a statement shared with FOX 12 on Friday. The Oregon Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory at Oregon State University confirmed an elevated viral load of EEHV the following day, leading the care team to administer plasma transfusions. Another baby elephant housed at the Oregon Zoo, 6-year-old Lily, succumbed to the virus in 2018. But staff say there’s hope this time. “Early detection is critical,” said Dr. Carlos Sanchez, the zoo’s animal health director.

items.x: PORTLAND, Ore. (KPTV) - Guard Ja Morant will be out for at least four weeks after suffering a hamstring injury, the Portland Trail Blazers announced Friday. Medals fill Meiler’s home in Shelburne. Most are gold, and a few are silver. How she started Meiler began competing at 60 when her friend Barbara Jordan convinced her to try the long jump at the Vermont Senior Games, and Meiler was hooked. Jordan died a decade ago. “I miss her so much,” Meiler said. Still competing at 91 Meiler continues to compete. “I’m sad that I can’t jump like I used to, but I really enjoy it,” she said. items.t: New study reveals 43% drop in childhood peanut allergies over last decade
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Recent research suggests that the long-held medical advice to avoid peanut products for young children may have been exactly the wrong approach. New studies indicate that introducing peanut products to infants between 4 and 6 months old can significantly reduce the risk of developing a peanut allergy. According to a study released in October 2025, peanut allergy rates in children under 3 have dropped by roughly 43% over the last decade. Dr. David Hill, lead author of the study, believes the reversal in guidance is a major factor in this decline. “It’s safe to say in all likelihood, there are tens of thousands of kids today that don’t have food allergy that may have if we hadn’t made these recommendations about early allergen introduction,” Dr. Hill said. items.x: OAK GROVE, Ore. (KPTV) - An elderly woman died Thursday after she was hit by a driver in Oak Grove, according to Oregon State Police. The crash happened at about 8:42 a.m. on Highway 99E. OSP said a driver in a white Kia Soul was going northbound near Holly Avenue when they hit 75-year-old Janice Mae Gilliland who was trying to cross the highway in an unmarked crosswalk. Detectives believe there may be more victims who have yet to come forward. Anyone with information about Lopez can contact the Investigations Division at 503-846-2500 and reference case number 50-26-14807.

items.t: Man convicted of killing wife in 2010 dies in Oregon prison
items.x: UMATILLA, Ore. (KPTV) - A man convicted of murdering his wife in 2010 died Thursday morning at a prison in Umatilla, according to the Oregon Department of Corrections. Namegabe Mushegero, who was serving a life sentence, died in the infirmary at Two Rivers Correctional Institution. He was 68. The DOC said state police have been notified and the medical examiner will determine the cause of death. His next of kin has been notified. Mushegero admitted to killing his wife, Nabintu Kalamba, in 2010 by beating her with a hammer inside their Washington County apartment in front of their children. He later pleaded guilty to murder and was sentenced to life in prison.

items.t: When ‘I’ll never put you in a home’ meets real-life caregiving
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Caregiving promises are sometimes made during emotional moments. When a loved one says, “I’ll never put you in a home,” or “You can always live with me,” the words may come from love, but health, safety, money and caregiver capacity can change over time. The Aging Untold experts explain why families may feel guilt or pressure later and what to say instead. Why promises can create pressure Families often make promises before they have talked through what caregiving could involve, Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said. “They haven’t looked at the reality and talked about the reality at first,” O’Rourke said. “You know, ‘I’ll take care of you.’ But if these certain things happen, we’re going to have to have another conversation.” She said the questions can be practical: Can we afford the care? items.t: ‘Bad houseguest’ in the attic: What to know about shingles symptoms and treatments
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Many people think the first sign of shingles is a bad rash, but it can start with intense pain in the body. ‘Intense amount of burning’ Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said she had shingles twice and it was tied to an autoimmune condition, and described the pain as burning. “It burned. It’s an infection in the nerve, essentially. It is nerve pain at the highest level,” Cradduck said. She compared it to a toothache. “You know how intense a toothache is. Now think about that in a pathway, in a nerve pathway in your body,” Cradduck said. Her pain was on her back and flank. “Not something I could see, not something I could reach, but just an intense amount of burning. And then it came around,” she said. items.t: This family runs a distillery in an old fire station
items.x: DALE, Wis. ( InvestigateTV ) — A Wisconsin family runs a distillery in an old fire station along Highway 96 in Dale, with a business designed to support the fire departments that keep them safe. Volunteer firefighter Alex Hopfensperger works at the family business, Old Station 31 Spirits. “Right now we’re distilling in-house vodka and gin, so we have the four vodkas and two gins,” Alex Hopfensperger said. “We wanted to become a part of the community, and 20-plus years ago, part of becoming part of the community was joining the volunteer fire department,” Rob Hopfensperger said. items.t: Students learn the power of giving through painting pet portraits
items.x: WINNECONNE, Wis. ( InvestigateTV ) — Seventh graders at Winneconne Middle School are painting pet portraits for a community project. Students in Susan Meunier’s new leadership class are tracing and painting portraits of pets. Vaughn Wurtz and her classmates are working on the project at the school. “We had to do a project for something to do with the community that benefits the community,” Wurtz said. Aubrey Salm and Paul Reinke helped come up with the idea. “We’re doing pet portraits for Go Fetch and we’re going to donate all of the money to the humane society,” Salm said. Meunier said the students are working hard on the portraits. “They are putting so much effort into it,” Meunier said. She said the students told Go Fetch in an interview, “It might not be the best painting but we’ll try our hardest.” Meunier said they are trying hard on everything. items.t: Better than blood? Researcher says new discovery could help save lives
items.x: KANSAS CITY, Mo. ( InvestigateTV ) — A doctor and research scientist at the University of Missouri-Kansas City said he has discovered a potential alternative to blood transfusions for people with severe blood loss. He calls the treatment “better than blood.” When someone experiences severe trauma, such as a car crash or gunshot wound, they risk bleeding to death. Blood transfusions are currently the best treatment to try to stop severe blood loss, also known as hemorrhagic shock. items.t: Westview volleyball coach balances first season as a mom with playoff run
items.x: ROCK CREEK, Ore. (KPTV) — Westview High School volleyball coach Janelle Bryant is in her 10th season as varsity head coach and her first as a mother. Her team enters the OSAA playoffs as the fifth seed with three senior captains. “The school community and athletic community has been really supportive because being a first-time mom and coaching back in the fall, it’s a lot to juggle,” Bryant said. Bryant is a North Salem alum and a special education resource teacher at Westview. “I was pregnant last season, it was an adjustment, but this season has been just balancing going back to work full-time, coaching full-time with the baby but we’re making it work!” Bryant said. items.t: How caregivers can keep dignity intact when conversations get tense
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Stress can turn into sharp words when you are a caregiver for someone you love. The Aging Untold experts are sharing advice on how to communicate in a way that keeps dignity intact, builds cooperation and helps caregivers reset when a conversation escalates. Step away before things escalate “Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the first move to make when it feels like a conversation is about to escalate is to leave the room. “You have to step away. You really do,” Cradduck said. “You’ve got to let yourself calm down.” Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said caregivers can take that step by removing themselves or getting help. “If you’re fantasizing about escaping, or noticing the yellow flags like you’re starting to get hot, shaky, your jaw’s tense, that’s a good time to go, ‘OK, my nervous system is at its limit,’” Ambrose said. items.t: What to look for in a clinical trial and why older adults should be included
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Clinical trials can be a proactive way to explore new treatments, but studies show older adults are often left out of them, even though many conditions affect older adults more often. The Aging Untold experts hosts are discussing what to look for when choosing a study and how to decide whether to take part. items.t: InvestigateTV+: Prison program helping veterans
items.x: ( InvestigateTV ) — InvestigateTV+ takes you inside a peer-led prison program helping incarcerated veterans rebuild purpose through discipline and mentorship and talk to the supporters who say it’s breaking the cycle. Plus, how art is helping dementia patients reconnect and communicate. Then, an unlikely dog-and-cat friendship brings comfort to one family. Helping veterans rebuild American Legion Veterans Memorial Post 432 at Elayn Hunt Correctional Center was the first prison-based American Legion post in Louisiana, helping incarcerated veterans heal and rebuild their lives. The program is recognized for a zero percent recidivism rate. No one from the post comes back to prison. items.t: Bringing cancer screening conversations to the salon chair
items.x: ANDRESON, S.C. ( InvestigateTV ) - Do you only go to the doctor when you have an ache or feel sick? For many women that answer can be “yes.” A 2025 survey said that every one in six women say they missed or may have missed a routine cancer screening within the past year. A South Carolina salon is partnering with a statewide health initiative to have important conversations about cancer screening with clients. Kimberly Cheatham, owner of Kreative Kimistry in Anderson, has joined the Pink Palmetto Project, an effort by the South Carolina Cancer Alliance focusing on breast and cervical cancer education. Cheatham said her clients often get personal with her. “They confide in me when they don’t even feel comfortable telling their families things and their friends, because they know that I have a connection to them,” Cheatham said. ( InvestigateTV ) — A 1-year-old dog named Blueberry and a 10-month-old cat named Meadow were adopted together after they met at the veterinary hospital run by Last Chance Animal Rescue in Waldorf, Maryland. Rachel Clarke, who adopted both animals, said Blueberry “loves to play, and she loves to snuggle.” She said Meadow is “a little more independent, but Blueberry goes where Meadow goes.” Laurie Jenkins, assistant director of Last Chance Animal Rescue, said both animals arrived with wounds to their extremities that required amputations. Hospital Manager Lauren Webb said she got a call about Blueberry on Christmas Eve. “We’ve got to help this dog. It’s Christmas Eve. We’ve got to pull out a miracle,” Webb recalled. items.t: How art therapy helps patients connect with caregivers
items.x: WILMINGTON, N.C. ( InvestigateTV ) — Some doctors and caregivers are using art to help people with memory loss stay calm, engaged and connected. Research published by the National Library of Medicine shows drawing and painting can sometimes stimulate memories in people with dementia and other neurological diseases. Mother and daughter paint together June Lederle and her daughter, Cathie Lederle, create artwork at a table in their Wilmington home most days. On the day of the interview, Cathie was painting a bottle purple, the color of Alzheimer’s awareness. Before moving in with her mother, Cathie lived in Richmond, Virginia, and had a career in a technical field. June said the first signs that something was wrong appeared in 2019, starting with forgetfulness and then repeating tasks. Cognitive testing later confirmed their fears.
